title: The Complete Guide to Renting a House in India
seoTitle: How to Rent a House in India: Full Guide
description: A stage-by-stage guide to renting a home in India: budget, area, viewings, verifying the owner, agreements, deposits, moving in and moving out well.
excerpt: Most rental regret comes from doing the right things in the wrong order. Here's the whole journey in sequence, from working out your budget to getting your deposit back.

author.name: The StayOnMap team
author.role: Renters who've moved across half a dozen Indian cities

faq.q: What should I do first when looking for a rental in India?
faq.a: Work out two numbers before you look at a single listing: your realistic monthly total (rent, maintenance, electricity, water, gas, internet, parking) and the lump sum you need on move-in day (deposit, first month, any brokerage, moving costs, basic setup). Then choose an area and test the commute at the hour you would actually travel. Picking a flat before you have done both is how most people end up unhappy in a perfectly nice apartment.

faq.q: Why are rental agreements in India almost always 11 months?
faq.a: Because of the Registration Act, 1908, which requires a lease of immovable property from year to year, or for a term exceeding one year, to be registered. An 11-month term falls below that threshold, so landlords use it to avoid registration and the stamp duty that varies by state. It is a convention rather than an obligation, and an unregistered agreement is weaker evidence if you later need to prove what was agreed.

faq.q: How much security deposit is normal, and is there a legal cap?
faq.a: Deposits vary enormously between cities and even between neighbourhoods, and local custom drives the number more than anything else. On the legal side, tenancy is a state subject. The Model Tenancy Act, 2021 recommends a cap of two months rent for residential premises, but it is a model law approved by the Union Cabinet for states to adopt, so it binds you only where your state has enacted it. Check your own state before assuming a cap applies.

faq.q: How do I check that the person showing me the flat actually owns it?
faq.a: Ask to see an ownership document such as a sale deed, property tax receipt or an electricity bill in the owner name, and match that name against a photo ID. If you are dealing with a relative, caretaker or someone holding a power of attorney, ask for that authority in writing. Pay by bank transfer, UPI or cheque to a named account, never cash, and never pay anything, including a token amount, for a property you have not seen in person.

faq.q: What should I photograph before I move in?
faq.a: Everything, while the flat is still empty. Every room from two angles, every existing scratch, stain, crack, damp patch and non-working fitting, all bathrooms and kitchen fittings, and the electricity and water meter readings. Share the photographs with the landlord the same day so there is a record they were received, and send one written message listing every defect you found. This is the single cheapest thing you can do to protect your deposit.

faq.q: What should I do in the last month before I move out?
faq.a: Read your notice clause and give written, dated notice with enough time, since notice periods of one to three months are common. Check for lock-in and for any painting or cleaning obligation you agreed to. On handover day, photograph the final meter readings and every room, clear all dues and collect receipts, and get a short written handover note recording the date, readings, keys returned, the refund amount and the date it will be paid. Agree the settlement before you hand over the keys.

body:
Priya took a job in Pune and gave herself one weekend to find a place. She landed on Friday night, saw nine flats on Saturday, liked the fourth one, and paid a token amount on Sunday evening so nobody else could take it.

The flat itself was fine. Genuinely fine — good light, decent water pressure, a landlord who answered his phone. The problem was everything around it. Her office was fourteen kilometres away, which sounds reasonable in a browser tab and turned out to be well over an hour each way once the flyover traffic got involved. No chemist within walking distance. A maintenance charge she hadn't thought to ask about. A deposit she was told was "standard for this area," with no way of knowing whether that was true.

She stayed eleven months and disliked ten of them.

Nothing Priya did was stupid. She did the right things in the wrong order — picked a flat and then discovered the area, worked out the total cost after committing to the rent, and read the agreement for the first time on the day she signed it.

Renting well in India isn't mostly about being a shrewd negotiator or knowing some obscure clause. It's about doing roughly ten things in the right sequence, and doing the cheap ones — the questions, the walk-arounds, the photographs, the reading — before the expensive ones.

This is that sequence. Every stage below gets the version you can act on this week, plus a link to the longer piece when you want the detail.

## The order, in one table

If you read nothing else, read this. Most rental regret traces back to a stage that got skipped or done out of turn.

| # | Stage | The mistake people make |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Work out what you can actually afford | Budgeting the rent, not the total |
| 2 | Choose the area | Choosing the flat first, area second |
| 3 | Find and read listings | Trusting photographs |
| 4 | View and inspect | Visiting once, at the wrong hour |
| 5 | Verify the owner | Paying before confirming who owns it |
| 6 | Agree the terms in writing | Reading the agreement at the signing table |
| 7 | Pay and document the deposit | No dated photos, no refund clause |
| 8 | Move in properly | No meter readings, no defect list |
| 9 | Live there | Verbal complaints, no paper trail |
| 10 | Leave properly | Handing over keys before settling the account |

Stages one to five cost you nothing but time. Stages six onwards cost you money. That's the whole argument for the order.

## Stage 1 — Work out what you can actually afford

Rent is not the cost of renting. It's the headline number, and it's usually somewhere between sixty and eighty percent of what leaves your account every month once everything else lands.

Sit down before you look at a single listing and write two figures. The first is your real monthly total: rent, society maintenance, electricity at whatever rate the meter is billed at, water if it isn't included, cooking gas, internet, and parking if it's charged separately. The second — the one that catches people out — is the lump sum you need on the day you move in. That's the deposit, the first month's rent, any brokerage, the moving van, and the unglamorous shopping list of a curtain rod, a gas connection and a new mattress.

The move-in lump sum is often several times a month's rent, and it's dead money for the length of your tenancy. If you're moving from one rental to another, you'll usually need the new deposit before the old one comes back. Plan for that overlap. A lot of otherwise sensible renters get squeezed hard in exactly that fortnight. The full list of what quietly adds up is in [the hidden costs of renting in India](/blog/hidden-costs-of-renting-in-india).

One more thing while you're still holding all the leverage: the number on the listing is an opening position, not a price. Rent is negotiable, and in many markets the deposit is *more* negotiable than the rent — especially on a flat that's been empty a while. Almost nobody asks. [How to negotiate rent without losing the flat](/blog/negotiating-rent-in-india) covers what actually works and when to keep quiet.

## Stage 2 — Choose the area before you choose the flat

Here's the pattern I'd bet on: people who dislike their rental almost never dislike the rooms. They dislike the journey to work, the walk home after dark, the fact that nothing useful is within walking distance, or the water tanker that shows up on somebody else's schedule.

You can change a flat's furniture. You cannot change where it is.

So do the boring test first. Travel from the area to wherever you'll go most often — office, campus, a parent's house — at the hour you'd actually travel, on a weekday. Not on Sunday morning when the road is empty. If the commute is by public transport, do it on public transport, including the last-mile bit that nobody mentions. If it's twenty minutes on a map and fifty in practice, you want to learn that before you sign, not in your second week.

Then walk the neighbourhood twice: once on a weekday evening, once on a weekend morning. You're looking for a chemist, a grocery, street lighting, how the last two hundred metres feel after nine at night, whether the road floods, and where the water comes from — corporation supply, borewell, or tankers. Ask a watchman or a shopkeeper; they have no reason to sell you anything.

Areas have personalities, and they change every kilometre or two. [How to read a city's areas, using Chennai as the worked example](/blog/best-areas-to-live-in-chennai) shows the method — it transfers to any city you're moving to.

## Stage 3 — Find the listings, and learn to read them

Listings in India live in more places than people expect. Portals and apps carry the volume, brokers carry a lot of what isn't online, and a serious share of good rentals never gets advertised at all — they move through society WhatsApp groups, watchmen, notice boards near the gate, and word of mouth. If you've picked an area first, you can work all of those. If you haven't, you can only work the portals.

Reading a listing is mostly noticing what isn't there. Wide-angle photos make small rooms look generous. Five photos of the living room and none of the bathroom or kitchen is telling you something. No photo of the building exterior usually means the building is the weak point. "Semi-furnished" has no standard meaning at all — get an actual list of what stays.

Two things should be stated plainly, and if they aren't, ask before you travel: the deposit and the monthly maintenance. A listing that gives you rent alone is hiding the two numbers most likely to change your decision. And an address that's vague on purpose — "prime location near IT park" — is either a broker protecting a lead or something worse.

Where the listing sits geographically matters more than how it's described, which is the case for looking at homes on a map instead of a scrolling list. That argument, and what it changes about how you search, is in [why maps beat lists for finding a home](/blog/why-maps-beat-lists-for-finding-a-home).

## Stage 4 — View it properly, and view it more than once

Go with a written list. Not because you'll forget the big things, but because you'll forget the small ones in the ninety seconds you spend feeling either impressed or disappointed.

Run every tap and check pressure at the top floor if that's where you'd live. Flush every toilet. Test every socket and switch you can reach. Look at ceilings and the wall behind cupboards for damp — the paint is often newest exactly where the problem is. Open the windows and listen. Check your phone signal in the bedroom. Find out where the water comes from, where the parking is, whether the lift has a backup, and what the building does about power cuts.

Then, if you're serious about the place, go back at a different time of day. A flat that's charming at eleven in the morning can be dark at four, or loud at eight, or impossible to park near at nine. This second visit is the cheapest insurance in the whole process, and it's the one people skip because they're afraid of losing the flat.

Take the full version with you: [the house-hunting inspection checklist](/blog/house-hunting-checklist-india). And separately, [the questions to ask before you rent](/blog/questions-to-ask-before-renting) — the ones about deposit refund timelines, notice periods, repairs and restrictions that are awkward to ask later and painless to ask now.

## Stage 5 — Make sure you're dealing with the real owner

This is the stage most renters skip entirely, and it's the one that turns a bad month into a lost year's savings.

Before any money moves, establish who has the right to rent the property. Ask to see an ownership document — a sale deed, a property tax receipt, an electricity bill in the owner's name — and check the name on it against a photo ID. If you're dealing with a relative, a caretaker or somebody holding a power of attorney, ask to see the authority in writing. A genuine owner finds this reasonable. Anyone who's offended by it is telling you something.

The classic frauds are all built on urgency and distance. A flat priced noticeably below everything around it. An "owner" who is out of town and wants a token amount to hold it, sight unseen. A pushy demand to pay cash today because there's another tenant deciding tonight. A refusal to meet in person at the property. Any one of those should stop the conversation; two together should end it.

Pay traceably — bank transfer, UPI or cheque — to a named account, and get a receipt for every rupee including the token. [How rental scams actually work in India, and how to spot them](/blog/rental-scams-in-india) walks through the common setups in detail. It's fifteen minutes that has saved people a great deal more.

## Stage 6 — The agreement, the 11-month convention, and registration

You've probably noticed that nearly every rental agreement in India runs for eleven months. There's a specific reason. Under the Registration Act, 1908, a lease of immovable property from year to year, or for a term exceeding one year, must be registered. An eleven-month term sits below that line, so landlords have historically used it to avoid registration and the associated stamp duty, which varies from state to state.

It's a convention, not a rule you're obliged to follow — and it has a cost for you. An unregistered agreement is weaker evidence if you ever need to prove what was agreed. Weigh the registration cost against the size of your deposit before deciding it isn't worth it.

On the wider legal picture, be careful about what you assume. Tenancy in India is a state subject, so the rules that bind you depend on where you live. The Model Tenancy Act, 2021 was approved by the Union Cabinet as a *model* law — a template circulated for states to adopt. It binds nobody on its own. Where a state has enacted it, or its own version, you get real machinery: written agreements, a rent authority, and a recommended cap of two months' rent as a residential security deposit. Where a state hasn't, none of that applies to you. Find out where your state actually stands rather than repeating what you read on a forum.

Whatever the term, get these in writing before you sign: the rent and due date, any escalation, the deposit amount with the refund timeline and the specific grounds for deduction, the notice period on both sides, any lock-in, who pays for what repairs, and what needs the landlord's permission. Read it somewhere other than at the signing table. [What belongs in an Indian rental agreement, clause by clause](/blog/rental-agreements-in-india) is the detailed version.

## Stage 7 — The deposit, and how to protect it

The security deposit is the largest cheque most renters write and the one they document least. That imbalance — not landlord villainy — is what causes most disputes at the end of a tenancy.

Two things protect you, and both happen at the start. First, the clause: the agreement should say the amount, the number of days within which it's refundable after you vacate, and what can legitimately be deducted. "Refundable on vacating" is not a term; it's a sentiment. Second, the evidence: before you move a single box in, walk the empty flat with your phone and photograph every room, every existing scratch, stain, crack and non-working fitting, plus the meters. Timestamped photos, ideally shared with the landlord that day so there's a record he received them.

Normal wear and tear is generally not deductible — faded paint and ageing fittings are the cost of a property being lived in. Actual damage is different. The argument almost never turns on that principle; it turns on nobody having documented the condition on day one. Whoever holds the money wins a memory contest.

[Security deposits in India, and how to get yours back](/blog/security-deposits-in-india) has the full move-in protocol and what to do if a refund stalls.

## Stage 8 — Moving in: the first week

The first week is the last cheap chance to put things on record. Do these before you unpack properly.

Photograph the electricity and water meter readings on the day you take possession, ideally with the landlord present, and note them in a message. Sort out utility accounts — either transferred to your name or with the readings clearly recorded so you never pay for the previous tenant's consumption. Register with the society or association, get your entry passes, parking allotment and gate protocols, and find out the rules about visitors, movers and deliveries before they become an argument.

Then send one message listing every defect you found: the tap that drips, the socket that doesn't work, the door that never closed properly. In writing, dated, however minor. This is the document that stops a pre-existing fault becoming your deduction in eighteen months.

Finally, start a folder — digital is fine. Agreement, receipts for every payment, the ID copies you handed over, your move-in photographs, the meter readings, and every message thread with the landlord. [The rental documents checklist](/blog/rental-documents-checklist) sets out exactly what to keep and for how long.

## Stage 9 — Living there: what you can expect, what you maintain

The broad convention across most Indian tenancies is that the landlord handles the structure and major fittings — the roof, the plumbing behind the walls, the wiring, the water tank, the geyser and appliances that came with the flat — and the tenant handles day-to-day upkeep and consumables: bulbs, tap washers, minor repairs, and anything the tenant breaks. But it's a convention, and your agreement can say otherwise, so what you signed matters more than what's usual.

A few habits pay for themselves. Report problems in writing, even when you've already called — a message thread is a record and a phone call isn't. Get acknowledgements in writing too; if the landlord agrees a leak is structural and his responsibility, you want that in text, because the conversation eighteen months from now will go differently. And don't withhold rent as leverage in a dispute, however satisfying it sounds; it usually converts a strong position into a weak one.

Where a state tenancy law is in force, you may also have specific protections around notice before the landlord enters, and a rent authority to approach. Where it isn't, your agreement and the general law are what you have. [Tenant rights in India, and their real limits](/blog/tenant-rights-in-india) is honest about which is which.

## Stage 10 — Leaving well, and getting the deposit back

Start earlier than feels necessary. Read your notice clause and count backwards; notice periods of one to three months are common, and giving notice a week late can cost you a month's rent. Put the notice in writing with the date, and keep a copy even if you also tell them in person.

Check for a lock-in period and for any painting or cleaning clause. Some agreements make the tenant liable for repainting regardless of condition — if yours does, you agreed to it, and the time to argue was before signing.

On handover day, do the reverse of your move-in: final meter readings photographed, all dues cleared with receipts, and a walk-through with the landlord where you photograph every room again. Then get a short written handover note — date of vacating, meter readings, keys returned, amount to be refunded, and the date it will be paid. Agree the settlement before the keys change hands. Once you've handed over the flat and left the city, your negotiating position is a phone call and a hope.

If you need to leave before the term is up, that's a separate problem with its own rules about lock-in, notice and forfeited deposits — [breaking a lease early in India](/blog/breaking-a-lease-in-india) covers how to do it with the least damage.

## What people get wrong most often

- **Falling for the flat before checking the area.** The rooms are never the reason people move out early.
- **Budgeting the rent instead of the total.** The monthly extras and the move-in lump sum are what hurt.
- **Paying anything before confirming who owns the property.** Including the token.
- **Reading the agreement at the signing table.** Ask for a copy a day early. A landlord who refuses that is a landlord you now know something about.
- **Verbal everything.** Complaints, agreements, permissions, notice. If it isn't written, it didn't happen.

## Where StayOnMap fits into this

Short and honest, because a rental platform can't solve most of the above for you.

Our homepage is a map rather than a list, which exists for one reason: it makes you pick an area before you pick a flat, which is the sequence this whole guide argues for. Every listing states rent, deposit and maintenance as required fields, so the two numbers most likely to change your mind are visible before you travel anywhere. There's no brokerage. And you contact the owner directly, which means the person answering your questions about the deposit is the person who'll be returning it.

That's the scope. Better information earlier, fewer people in between. The photographs, the questions and the paperwork are still yours to do.

## What to remember

The order is the whole thing. Money and area before flat. Questions before payment. Reading before signing. Photographs before boxes.

The law is uneven and local — tenancy is a state subject, and the Model Tenancy Act, 2021 only means something where your state has enacted it. Check your own state's position instead of assuming a national rule protects you.

And almost all of your leverage exists before you move in. After that, you're negotiating with someone who's holding your money.

Priya rents in a different part of Pune now. She spent three weeks on it instead of one weekend, did the commute twice before she shortlisted anything, and photographed the empty flat before a single box came up the stairs.

She's still there. That's the entire difference.
